1.title: ADM PHASES B, C & D — THE ARCHITECTURE DOMAINS
1.text: Welcome to Module 4. With the Vision approved in Phase A, we now roll up our sleeves and actually develop the architecture — across three phases and four domains. Phase B is Business. Phase C is Information Systems, which is Data plus Application. And Phase D is Technology. There's a lot of ground here, but here's the good news: these three phases all share the same underlying structure. So we'll learn that structure once, then apply it to each domain in turn. Let's begin.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's the plan. You'll learn the shared structure that's common to Phases B, C, and D — because mastering it once saves you three times over. You'll learn to perform a gap analysis using the baseline-and-target matrix, which is a genuine exam favourite. You'll describe Phase B and its modern anchors, capabilities and value streams. You'll describe Phase C, which is Data plus Application. You'll describe Phase D, Technology. And you'll be able to name representative artifacts for each domain. Above all, focus on that common nine-step structure — it's the single highest-value idea in this module.

1.title: The Three Domain Phases at a Glance
1.text: Let's get the lay of the land. Phase B develops the Business domain — strategy, organization, processes, and capabilities. Phase C develops Information Systems, and that means two domains: Data and Application. Phase D develops Technology — the platforms, infrastructure, and standards. And all three follow the same overall approach: they take the Vision, develop a baseline and a target, perform gap analysis, and define candidate roadmap components. Two things to remember from this slide: Phase C is two domains in one, and the usual order is B then C then D — though, as always, that order is tailorable to your situation.

1.title: The Shared Structure of Phases B, C & D
1.text: Here's the structure worth memorizing — the nine steps that each domain phase follows, identically. One, select your reference models, viewpoints, and tools. Two, develop the baseline architecture description — the as-is. Three, develop the target architecture description — the to-be. Four, perform gap analysis between them. Five, define candidate roadmap components from those gaps. Six, resolve impacts across the architecture landscape. Seven, conduct a formal stakeholder review. Eight, finalize the architecture. And nine, create or update the Architecture Definition Document. This exact nine-step pattern is the same for Business, for Information Systems, and for Technology. Learn it once here, and you've effectively learned all three phases.

1.title: Baseline-First or Target-First?
1.text: Within those steps, there's a choice about sequencing — do you develop the baseline first or the target first? Baseline-first means you document the as-is state and then derive the target from it; that works well for stable, well-understood areas where the current state is worth capturing carefully. Target-first means you design the to-be state and then map back to the baseline; that suits genuine transformation, where dwelling on the old way adds little value. The choice depends on the maturity and stability of the area you're architecting. And the exam point is simply that TOGAF supports both orderings — there's no single mandated direction.

1.title: The Gap Analysis Technique
1.text: Now the technique that sits at the heart of every domain phase — gap analysis. Its basic premise is to highlight the shortfall between the Baseline Architecture and the Target Architecture: the things that have been deliberately omitted, accidentally left out, or simply not yet defined. It's used across Phases B, C, and D, and the technique itself is documented in the ADM Techniques material. And here's a lovely insight from the standard: the most critical source of gaps is stakeholder concerns that haven't been addressed in prior architectural work. As the matrix on screen shows, gap analysis is fundamentally about asking, honestly, what might we have forgotten?

1.title: How to Read the Gap Analysis Matrix
1.text: Let's actually read the matrix, because the exam can ask about its mechanics. You put the Baseline architecture building blocks down the vertical axis, and the Target building blocks across the horizontal axis. Then you add one extra row labelled "New" and one extra column labelled "Eliminated." Now you fill in the cells. Where a building block appears in both baseline and target, you mark it "Included." Where a baseline block is missing from the target, you mark it in the "Eliminated" column — and you check whether that removal was intentional or an accidental omission. And where a target block has no match in the baseline, you mark it against the "New" row — that's a gap to be developed or procured. The rule: anything under "New" or "Eliminated" is a gap that must be explained or filled.

1.title: Phase B — Business Architecture: Objectives
1.text: Let's start working through the domains, beginning with Phase B, Business Architecture. Its objective is to develop the Target Business Architecture — a description of how the enterprise needs to operate to achieve the agreed Vision — and to identify candidate roadmap components from the gaps between baseline and target. There's an important reason Phase B usually comes first among the domains: the Business Architecture demonstrates the business value of the whole effort, and it provides the foundation that the Data, Application, and Technology work all build upon. So Phase B isn't just first by alphabet — it's first because it justifies everything that follows.

1.title: Phase B — Business Capabilities
1.text: A central concept in modern TOGAF Business Architecture is the business capability. A capability is a particular ability or capacity that the business possesses, or needs to possess — and crucially, it describes the "what," not the "how." For example, "claims processing" or "customer onboarding" are capabilities; they say what the business can do without prescribing how it's done or who does it. Capability mapping gives you a stable, outcome-based view of the enterprise that doesn't churn every time you reorganize. You capture these in a Business Capabilities catalog and a Business Capability Map. The exam-relevant essence: a capability is about what the business can do, independent of how, or who.

1.title: Phase B — Value Streams
1.text: The partner concept to capabilities is the value stream. A value stream is an end-to-end set of value-adding activities that creates an overall outcome for a customer or stakeholder. You break it into value stream stages, and each stage is enabled by one or more business capabilities. That linkage is so useful that it's often captured explicitly in a Value Stream to Capability matrix, showing which capabilities power which stages of value delivery. Together, value streams and capabilities are the two modern anchors of TOGAF 10 Business Architecture — value streams show how value flows, and capabilities show what's needed to deliver it. Expect the exam to pair them.

1.title: Phase B — Organization Maps & Other Concepts
1.text: Rounding out Phase B's toolkit is the Organization Map, which shows the organizational units and how they relate to capabilities and value streams. Beyond those headline three, Phase B also works with business services, functions, processes, products, drivers, goals, and objectives — the familiar furniture of business modeling. And it reuses the business scenarios technique from Phase A, now applied at a more detailed level. If you remember three Phase B viewpoints for the exam, make them the Organization Map, the Capability Map, and the Value Stream — those are the headline three that define TOGAF 10's approach to the business domain.

1.title: Phase B — Representative Artifacts
1.text: Let's note some representative Phase B artifacts, grouped by the three families you already know. Catalogs — lists of things — include the Organization and Actor catalog, the Driver-Goal-Objective catalog, the Role catalog, and the Business Capabilities and Value Stream catalogs. Matrices — showing relationships — include the Business Interaction matrix, the Actor-Role matrix, and the Value Stream to Capability matrix. And diagrams — pictures — include the Business Footprint diagram, the Functional Decomposition diagram, and the Capability, Value Stream, and Organization maps. You don't need to memorize every one, but do remember the three families: catalogs are lists, matrices are relationships, diagrams are pictures.

1.title: Phase C — Information Systems Architectures
1.text: On to Phase C, the one with the famous twist. Its purpose is to develop the Information Systems Architectures that support the Vision — and that means two sub-architectures, Data and Application. These can be developed in either order, or concurrently, depending on what's driving the work. Whatever the order, Phase C must show how the information systems enable the Business Architecture from Phase B and serve the overall Vision. I'll keep saying it because the exam keeps testing it: Phase C equals Data plus Application. If a question asks where Data Architecture is developed, or where Application Architecture is developed, the answer to both is Phase C.

1.title: Data Before Application — or Vice Versa?
1.text: Let's address the ordering within Phase C, since it sometimes appears in questions. TOGAF lets you develop either the Data Architecture or the Application Architecture first. Data-first is common when data is the primary concern — think master data management or analytics initiatives, where getting the data model right comes first. Application-first is common when the applications are what's really driving the design. And very often the two are developed concurrently, with frequent cross-checks between them. The exam takeaway: there's no fixed order within Phase C. It depends entirely on the enterprise's drivers, so beware any answer claiming one must always precede the other.

1.title: Phase C — Data Architecture
1.text: Let's look at the Data Architecture half of Phase C. It defines the structure of the organization's logical and physical data assets, along with the data management resources. Its central concern is data entities — what they are, how they relate to each other, and crucially, which applications and business functions actually use them. Two guiding principles tend to apply: data is an asset to be shared across the enterprise, and redundancy should be avoided. And here's a clean distinction to hold onto: Data Architecture is about the data itself — its structure and meaning — not about the database technology that stores it. The storage technology is a Phase D concern.

1.title: Phase C — Data Architecture Artifacts
1.text: A few representative Data Architecture artifacts. The main catalog is the Data Entity and Data Component catalog — your list of data entities. The matrices include the Data Entity to Business Function matrix and the Application to Data matrix, which show which functions and applications touch which data. And the diagrams include the Conceptual and Logical Data diagrams, the Data Security diagram, the Data Migration diagram, and the Data Lifecycle diagram. One worth remembering by name is the Data Dissemination diagram, which shows how data entities map to applications and where the data physically lives. If a question describes mapping data to the applications that use it, think Data Dissemination diagram.

1.title: Phase C — Application Architecture
1.text: Now the Application Architecture half. It provides a blueprint of the individual applications, how they interact with one another, and how they relate to the core business processes. The key thing to grasp is the level of abstraction: this is about logical applications — often called application components — not about the technology that runs them. TOGAF even notes that applications should be relatively stable and unchanging, because they describe what the applications do, not how they're built. So lock in this distinction: Application Architecture defines logical application components, and it's deliberately technology-independent. The actual platforms come in Phase D.

1.title: Phase C — Application Architecture Artifacts
1.text: Representative Application Architecture artifacts now. The catalogs include the Application Portfolio catalog — your master list of applications — and the Interface catalog. The matrices include the Application to Organization matrix, the Role to Application matrix, the Application to Function matrix, and the Application Interaction matrix. And the diagrams include the Application and User Location diagram, the Application Use-Case diagram, and the Process to Application Realization diagram. The one to remember by name is the Application Communication diagram, which shows the applications and the communications flowing between them. So: Application Communication diagram for how apps talk to each other.

1.title: Phase D — Technology Architecture: Objectives
1.text: On to Phase D, Technology Architecture. Its objective is to develop the Target Technology Architecture that enables the business, data, and application services defined in the earlier phases — and, like the others, to identify candidate roadmap components from the gaps. It describes the logical and physical technology: the platforms, the networks, the infrastructure, and importantly the standards that everything must conform to. Think of Phase D as the foundation layer of the whole stack. Everything above it — business, data, applications — ultimately runs on the technology architecture you define here. It's where the abstract services finally meet real infrastructure.

1.title: Phase D — Key Concepts & Reference Models
1.text: Phase D leans on reference models to get started, and the headline one is the Technical Reference Model, the TRM. The TRM gives you a generic taxonomy of platform services to work from, so you're not starting with a blank page. Phase D is also where you define your technology standards — captured in something called the Standards Information Base — and your platform services, while keeping an eye on emerging technologies and any constraints. We'll cover the TRM properly in Module 13, but for now just remember the link: the Technical Reference Model provides a model of generic platform services, and it's a natural starting point for Phase D.

1.title: Phase D — Technology Architecture Artifacts
1.text: Representative Technology Architecture artifacts. The catalogs include the Technology Standards catalog and the Technology Portfolio catalog — your inventory of technology in use. The key matrix is the Application to Technology matrix, mapping applications onto the technology that supports them. And the diagrams include the Environments and Locations diagram, the Processing diagram, and the network and hardware diagrams. The one to remember by name is the Platform Decomposition diagram, which depicts the technology platform underpinning the whole architecture. So if a question describes a picture of the underlying technology platform, that's your Platform Decomposition diagram.

1.title: Gap Analysis Across B, C & D
1.text: Let's bring gap analysis back, because each domain phase ends with it, and the kinds of gaps differ by domain. In the Business domain, you look for people gaps, process gaps, tools gaps, information gaps, measurement gaps, financial gaps, and even facilities gaps. In the Data domain, you look for data that's wrong, out of date, or missing — data not available where or when it's needed. And in the Application and Technology domains, you look for components that are impacted, eliminated, or newly created. Whatever the domain, the punchline is the same: the gaps you find become the candidate roadmap components that feed into Phase E.

1.title: The Architecture Definition Document (ADD)
1.text: A document we met in Module 2 grows up across these phases — the Architecture Definition Document, or ADD. Each domain phase creates or updates it. The ADD is the qualitative description of your architecture: the baseline and target across all the domains, together with the rationale for your decisions. Its companion is the Architecture Requirements Specification, which carries the quantitative, measurable requirements. The key insight for the exam is that B, C, and D progressively populate the ADD — it isn't written in one go. It grows, phase by phase, as each domain adds its piece of the overall architecture description.

1.title: Candidate Roadmap Components
1.text: Let's talk about what each domain phase hands forward — candidate Architecture Roadmap components. Every phase, having found its gaps, defines the work those gaps imply, expressed as candidate roadmap components. As you move through Business, Data, Application, and Technology, these accumulate into a consolidated, cross-domain roadmap. But note the word "candidate" — at this stage they're proposals, not a finished plan. The actual refinement and sequencing happens later, in Phases E and F. So the clean division to remember is: B, C, and D propose roadmap components; E and F consolidate and plan them into a real schedule.

1.title: How Interoperability Builds Across the Phases
1.text: Here's a thread that weaves through all these phases — interoperability, the ability to share information and services. It isn't decided in one place; it's progressively defined across the ADM. In Phase A, it's first revealed within the business scenarios. In Phase B, it's defined in business terms. In Phase C's Data Architecture, you detail the content of the information exchanges. In Phase C's Application Architecture, you specify how applications share information and services. And in Phase D, you specify the technical mechanisms that actually permit those exchanges. So if the exam asks where interoperability is handled, the richer answer is that it's refined domain by domain, all the way through.

1.title: Common Thread — Stakeholder Review
1.text: One more shared thread before we summarize: every domain phase includes a formal stakeholder review before the architecture is finalized. This review checks the developing architecture against the Statement of Architecture Work and against the stakeholders' concerns, making sure everything still aligns before the cycle moves on toward planning. It's a quality gate. So the tail end of each B, C, and D phase follows the same little rhythm: stakeholder review, then finalize, then update the Architecture Definition Document. Three steps, repeated in each domain — another instance of that shared structure paying off.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Let's clear this module's traps. One: "Data Architecture is Phase B" — no, Data and Application are both Phase C. Two: "Application Architecture defines the technology platform" — no, that's Phase D; Phase C applications are logical. Three: "Phase C must do Data before Application" — no, either order is fine. Four: "gap analysis is only a Phase E activity" — no, it runs in B, C, and D. And five: "the ADD is finished in Phase A" — no, it's progressively built through the domain phases. The defence against all of these is to keep your domain-to-phase mapping crisp: B is Business, C is Data plus Application, D is Technology. Say it until it's reflex.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Your Module 4 cheat-sheet. The domain phases are B, C, and D. Phase C has two sub-architectures — Data and Application. Each phase shares the same nine steps. The core validation technique is gap analysis, with baseline ABBs as rows and target ABBs as columns. The gap markers are Included, Eliminated, and New. Phase B's anchors are capabilities and value streams. Phase D's reference model is the TRM. And the document built across all three phases is the Architecture Definition Document. Capture this slide — it distils three phases' worth of facts onto a single card.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's recap. Phases B, C, and D develop the BDAT architectures, and all three share the same nine-step structure. Gap analysis — baseline building blocks against target building blocks, with New and Eliminated markers — exposes the shortfalls. Phase B uses capabilities and value streams; Phase C is Data plus Application, in either order; Phase D leans on the Technical Reference Model. Each phase produces candidate roadmap components and updates the Architecture Definition Document. And both interoperability and the ADD are built up progressively across the domains rather than all at once. That's the engine room of the ADM.

1.title: Bridge to Module 5
1.text: So where does all this lead? Having finished Phases B, C, and D, we're left with a target architecture and a substantial pile of gaps and candidate roadmap components. Phase E, Opportunities and Solutions, takes those gaps and turns them into work packages and Transition Architectures — the deliverable building blocks of change. Then Phase F, Migration Planning, sequences everything into a detailed, agreed plan. In other words, the roadmap components we just generated are the raw material that Phases E and F shape into an actual delivery roadmap. That's exactly where Module 5 picks up.

1.title: Quick Self-Check
1.text: Before the practice questions, a quick self-check. From memory: can you list the nine shared steps of a domain phase? Can you draw the gap analysis matrix and correctly mark New, Eliminated, and Included? Can you name two artifacts each for Business, Data, Application, and Technology? And can you say which reference model Phase D uses? If any of those came out hesitant, that's your cue to scroll back and re-watch the relevant slide before testing yourself. Honest self-checking now is what turns recognition into the fast, confident recall you need on exam day.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question 1. Which architecture domains are developed in ADM Phase C? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Data and Application Phase C — Information Systems Architectures develops both the Data Architecture and the Application Architecture. Business is Phase B; Technology is Phase D.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question 2. In the TOGAF gap analysis technique, what does an entry in the "New" row indicate? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is C. A target building block not found in the baseline — a gap to be developed or procured The "New" row captures Target ABBs that are not present in the Baseline — these are gaps that must be developed or procured. A building block in both is "Included"; one removed from the target is "Eliminated."

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question 3. Which two concepts are the central anchors of Business Architecture in TOGAF 10's Phase B? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Business capabilities and value streams TOGAF 10 emphasizes business capabilities (what the business can do) and value streams (end-to-end value-adding activities) as the central anchors of Phase B Business Architecture. The others belong to Phases C, D, and E.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question 4. Phases B, C, and D share a common structure. Which of the following is part of that shared structure? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is A. Develop baseline and target descriptions, then perform gap analysis Each domain phase follows the same pattern: select models/viewpoints/tools, develop baseline and target descriptions, perform gap analysis, define roadmap components, review, finalize, and update the ADD. The Architecture Contract is Phase G, the Migration Plan is Phase F, and the Request for Architecture Work triggers Phase A.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question 5. In Phase C, the Application Architecture describes applications primarily as: Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Logical application components, independent of the technology that runs them Application Architecture defines logical application components — what the applications do and how they interact — independent of the underlying technology. The physical technology platform is the concern of Phase D (Technology Architecture).
